newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Analysts warn over price for low Slovak inflation.
newsitem.headline: Analysts warn over price for low Slovak inflation.

text.p: Slovak consumer inflation rose 0.4 percent, month-on-month, putting prices 6.0 percent higher than the previous year, the Slovak Statistical Bureau (SUSR) said on Tuesday.
Analysts said the figures were satisfactory, but warned against undue optimism, saying inflation so far had been curbed mainly thanks to significantly high credit interest rates.
"I think we are at a critical point right now and further development could be either disastrous or good," Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst at bank CSOB told Reuters.

Though SUSR changed its methodology for calculating CPI at the beginning of the year and has not issued revised 1996 figures, Kuklis said inflation has been rising regularly by almost exactly 0.2 percent monthly since the second half of last year.
Consumer prices grew by 1.1 percent, month-on-month, in January, with the year-on-year, rate at 5.8 percent.

"The fact that inflation has been growing for a relatively long time is more serious than the latest figures. If we also take privatisation into account, there are many things on the horizon to look out for," he said.

SUSR said that due to changes in the population's spending structure, it had revised the formulae for calculating CPI in 1997, using 1995 data as a base. It also added some new items to the inflation basket, and modified others.
Boris Brnak of Creditanstalt warned that due to price deregulation in some areas, and controls in others, inflation figures are not fully indicative of price development.
"The latest growth in inflation is not serious," Brnak said. "But further development, such as energy prices, will show much more in this respect," he added.
Analysts also said the risk stemming from the high interest rates was increased by murky privatisations and a lack of direct foreign investment in Slovakia.
A large number of companies have been privatised in Slovakia over the last several years through credit, generating little income for the state, making it more difficult for it to support prices.
